newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Kabila's troops allow protest, marchers seize guns.
newsitem.headline: Kabila's troops allow protest, marchers seize guns.

text.p: Laurent Kabila's troops allowed over 1,000 protesters to march through the capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo on Friday in defiance of a government ban, but marchers seized guns from two soldiers who fired in the air.

Troops kept a close eye on the march and allowed it to pass through the city centre, but witnesses said that as protesters reached the suburban home of veteran opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi, two soldiers fired in the air and then were surrounded by the crowd.
"The soldiers were not hurt and walked off, but the crowd took their guns and they still have them," said one witness. It was not clear why the soldiers fired into the air.

Kabila and his government, which took office last month after the overthrow of President Mobutu Sese Seko, held a cabinet meeting in the southern mining city of Lubumbashi, 1,600 km (1,000 miles) from Kinshasa, officials said.
Protesters loyal to Tshisekedi, who has been excluded from Kabila's government, carried flags and banners which read "No to dictatorship" and "Kabila must go".

They also called for the departure of ethnic Tutsi Rwandan troops who helped ensure Kabila's success in a seven-month bush war to topple Mobutu, who dominated Africa's third largest country for three decades.

"We have marched today against dictatorship, to say no to a single party state and no to the suspension of political parties," Adrien Phongo, secretary-general of Tshisekedi's Union for Democracy and Social Progress party told the marchers. "We must struggle as one man before it is too late."
Last week troops opened fire to disperse anti-Kabila protesters.

National radio published a warning from the National Information Agency, which has taken over from Mobutu's feared SNIP security police, that action would be taken against anyone taking part in a demonstration.

"All demonstrations are forbidden, without exception," the radio said. One of the first acts of Kabila's government was to ban political activity and demonstrations, while promising to hold elections in April 1999.

The United States welcomed Kabila's election pledge and U.S. embassy officials in Kinshasa said envoy Bill Richardson would arrive in the capital on Friday afternoon before meeting with Kabila, probably in Lubumbashi.

Lubumbashi, in Kabila's home province of Katanga, is the centre of Congo's copper and cobalt mining region, which many business analysts see as the key to relaunching an economy ruined by years of political chaos and corruption.
Earlier on Friday a gang of around 100 youths rampaged in the centre of Kinshasa, smashing windows and throwing stones, to protest against a drop in the value of the local currency.

They did not claim links with either Tshisekedi or Kabila and accused Lebanese traders of conspiring to force the rate of exchange to 150,000 new zaires to the dollar, from around 120,000 on Thursday.
"The Lebanese were always conspiring with Mobutu and now they are trying to ruin the money," shouted one youth.
Inflation was a perennial problem in Mobutu's Zaire, where succesive governments resorted to the printing presses at the national mint whenever they were short of cash.
Kabila's government, whose arrival strengthened the new zaire, says it will follow a strict monetary policy and will at an unspecified date introduce a new currency, the Congolese franc.
